entry.title: On things that are touchingly earnest
entry.content:
There are all kinds of stories and images out there, but the ones I'm weakest against are the ones that strike me as touchingly earnest. The feelings a dog turns toward another dog, another animal, or its owner. A small child trying with everything they have to do something. A young person, their strength not yet fully grown in, giving it all they've got.

These things come across better with hardly any words. If someone did something touchingly earnest while narrating it, "Here I am, small and weak, still bravely trying," I might find myself a little put off, even if it were a dog or a baby.

I suspect we pick up on this quality more easily when the one doing the trying is small and cute and weak, but it lives in the actions of the rough and the strong, too. Either way, you can't help wanting to cheer them on: don't give up, keep going.

Meanwhile, the me who's feeling all this isn't actually lending a hand. I'm only letting my heart be moved, the way I would by a film or a story. I'm not doing anything that helps. "Earnestness like that is a wonderful thing," I think, and maybe, like a believer gazing up at a holy statue, I'm really just making sure of what lies at the very center of my own heart.

We can't really become touchingly earnest anymore. Puppies can, babies can, most weak things can, but it seems unlikely that we ever will, from here on. One reason is that we can talk, and talk far too much. Whether or not we say things well, we simply have too many words. Another is that we can't keep pushing past our limits forever. Faced with things that don't work out, with efforts that go unrewarded, we've learned how to give up, how to decide it's all a bit ridiculous. People like us probably can't be touchingly earnest anymore. And yet there's plenty that people like us can do precisely because of what we are, and taking on those roles matters too, you know.

If you have any thoughts, I'd love it if you sent me an email or something.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. This one's a bit hard to read, but, well, some days are like that.
entry.summary: The essay argues that we are most moved by the unguarded earnestness of small, weak, or striving beings, like puppies, children, and young people, yet adults have lost the capacity for such sincerity through overthinking and learned resignation. Still, the author suggests that grown people have other meaningful roles to play.

entry.title: Respect, but not submission
entry.content:
You mustn't take it lightly, and you mustn't be held captive by it. Honestly, you can say that about most things.

Take the economy, for instance. You mustn't take it lightly, and you mustn't be held captive by it. By which I mean money, profit, that sort of thing. You can flip the order, too: you mustn't be held captive by the economy, and you mustn't take it lightly.

Interestingly, almost everything people speak of as important fits this phrasing.

You mustn't take freedom lightly, and you mustn't be held captive by freedom. Both happen all the time.

You mustn't take family lightly, and you mustn't be held captive by family. I think there's plenty of both.

You mustn't take love lightly, and you mustn't be held captive by love. Either way, it's no good.

You mustn't take knowledge lightly, and you mustn't be held captive by knowledge. You see both of these often enough.

Hold respect for the things that matter, but don't submit to them. That's the attitude. I'm making it today's title.

If any thoughts come to mind, send me an email or something.

Thank you for coming by Hobonichi again today.

The more important something is, the easier it is to take it lightly, and the easier it is to be held captive by it, isn't it?
entry.summary: Important things can be mishandled in two opposite ways: taking them lightly or becoming captive to them. The essay argues for holding them with respect while refusing to submit to them.

entry.title: Come to think of it, it goes back to when I was a kid: on paper airplanes
entry.content:
Sometimes a kid who plays Little League keeps at it through high school and eventually becomes a pro ballplayer. When I stop and think about my own life, I find myself wondering whether what I do now is really the same thing I've been doing ever since elementary school.

There's a memory about a paper airplane that I've never forgotten. I was in fifth grade or so. One day I folded a sheet of memo paper into a plane, and it came out beautifully. It flew astonishingly well. I'd folded it the way I always did, so it was pure luck, but it glided through the air for so long, so smoothly, that I just stood there admiring it.

My classmates were impressed too, and soon everyone was grabbing whatever paper was lying around and folding planes of their own. But theirs didn't exactly sail along the way mine had. It seemed the palm-sized memo pad I had, the kind where you tear off one sheet at a time, was just the right paper for the job. I handed out sheets to my friends one by one, but we were all playing so eagerly that before long we ran out.

So I went to the little shop at school that sold stationery and bought a whole new pad. Here, everybody, use this! Now we can make as many paper airplanes as we want. (No, no, I wasn't some rich kid or anything.) We could hold contests to see whose plane flew the farthest. The craze didn't last all that long, but for a while we were all completely absorbed in that game.

I wanted to play some new kind of game, so I tried to build the "playground" for it, the system, you might say. Handing out the equipment, that sort of thing. I've been doing that all along. Maybe what I was doing with those paper airplanes was my version of Little League.

Who'd have thought that at my age I'd be looking back on what I've done with my life like this... huh.

If anything comes to mind, any thoughts or impressions at all, please send me an email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today.

Everyone has their own thing, don't they? Some people love gardening, some love playing house.
entry.summary: The writer reflects on a childhood paper airplane episode, where he bought a new pad of paper so everyone could keep playing, and sees it as his early version of "Little League": a lifelong pattern of building the systems and equipment that let others play.

entry.title: The flow of things: hard to explain, and that's the fun of it
entry.content:
There's this thing called "the flow," isn't there? As in "the flow of the game," or "we need to change the flow..." Everyone involved gets swept up in a shared picture, one with no real basis but heavy with a sense of what's coming. "When things are like this, this is how they go," and somehow everybody just decides it together. The flow is a story we're expecting, and sometimes it's also a dream we've seen many times before.

But even when things don't go the way the flow foretold, nobody seems to mind much. "The flow was pointing the other way, you know," people say, explaining the result after the fact. There was never any basis for it to begin with, so that's fine.

I'm rather fond of this faith in the flow. There's the pleasure of giving yourself over to it, and the pleasure of resisting it. It's a bit like saying "it was meant to be" or "I felt the hand of fate." When you sense a good flow and decide to ride it, the flow often seems to get even better. Probably because other people are sensing that "good flow" too, and they try to help it along. And then, if I'm being level-headed about it, when what was supposed to be a "good flow" ends in failure, people pick themselves up with an "Oh well" or a "So close." "We got pretty far, though," that sort of thing. Maybe I've simply "flowed" my way here myself, without ever really working out what I think about the flow at all.

It's nothing terribly important, but right now there's a big flow running through my life. A flow has come along urging me to walk. From books, from shoes, from horoscopes, from what the people around me are up to, there's a flow telling me I ought to walk more. If I make a grand resolution and set off with gusto, I'll get bored in no time, so I'm easing into it slowly, like soaking my feet in a footbath of that flow. It isn't a bad thing, after all, so I'm going to ride it and see where it goes. Only, now that I'm finally in the mood, the winter cold has come rushing in, as if to push back against the current.

If you have any thoughts on this piece, I'd love it if you sent me an email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today.

Come to think of it, the Japanese word for "trend" is written with the character for "flow," too. A fashion is just another kind of flow.
entry.summary: The essay examines "the flow," the shared, unfounded sense that events are heading in a particular direction, which people readily embrace and then rationalize after the fact when it fails. The author admits to being fond of this faith while questioning whether they've simply drifted along with it, using their own renewed urge to walk as an example.

entry.title: Not that I don't badmouth people myself
entry.content:
When someone talks trash about another person without holding back, nothing really happens as long as they're doing it alone. Even if two or three people are badmouthing someone to their hearts' content, if it never reaches the person being talked about, it probably doesn't go so far as to hurt anyone. And if, in some corner of some region of Japan, the locals were cursing somebody up and down, I doubt it would have had much of an effect either. "Oh, him? He's got a bad name around here." That sort of thing happens all the time.

Now suppose that at some point, somewhere, there was a big wall, and everyone started writing insults on it. Maybe they'd even give it a name, something like "the Badmouth Wall." Suddenly the trash talk that used to pass between two or three people can be read by everyone who walks by. "Go over there and you can read the dirt on somebody." Before long it turns into a kind of entertainment in rather poor taste, and it might even become a tourist attraction of the darker sort. Whoever scrawls the juiciest insults, the ones most likely to catch people's interest, could end up a dark hero of sorts, the toast of the town. True or false, clean or filthy, it doesn't matter. Badmouthing has impact, and there's something in it that draws people in.

Even I, sitting here writing this, have to admit there are insults I'd go and read with a rather unsavory "Ooh, let's have a look." I'm especially drawn to trash talk about people I don't care for, or about people who dislike me.

In the world since the internet took hold, the Badmouth Wall has become a business, and a place where people throw stones to blow off steam, where you can write just about anything you like. Even when it's about someone I dislike, I often find myself thinking, "You can really say that?!" Is it really all right for people to be badmouthed so freely? I don't think it is, not even when it's someone I can't stand, or an enemy. The internet has become an unpleasant place, I think, and all I can do is resolve that, at the very least, I won't take part in it myself.

If you'd like, please send me an email with your thoughts.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. I may be full of rudeness and impertinence, but even so, I do believe courtesy matters.
entry.summary: The essay argues that badmouthing only becomes harmful when it's broadcast publicly, like insults scrawled on a "Badmouth Wall," which the internet has turned into a business. The author admits to being drawn to such talk yet concludes it is wrong and resolves not to take part in it.

entry.title: So afraid of empty time that I got rid of it, and then...
entry.content:
I feel a great many things, think a great many things, turn a great many things over in my mind. And I also feel that I wish I had more empty time. Which gets me thinking about empty time. Which in turn gets me wondering what I ought to do with empty time. See? There I go again, thinking. Filling up the precious empty time I had. This is a kind of illness, probably. It's my illness, and the illness of everyone living in this day and age. We can't bear empty time.

Back when I was in elementary school or so, I had empty time. With nothing else for it, I'd often just lie there staring at the ceiling. Not television, not manga or books, just the ceiling, or sometimes the chest of drawers, or the sliding paper doors. "Why do they call a chest of drawers a chest of drawers?" I'd wonder, again and again, and then give it up. But that question, "Why do they call a chest of drawers a chest of drawers?", may well be where all my thinking began.

Empty time made me restless, and its blankness was hard to bear. How could I fill it? How could I make it go away? That's all I ever thought about, and I schemed, experimented, and put plan after plan into action. For decades upon decades, that's all I've been doing.

There are passive ways to erase empty time, too. You can just watch TV or read manga. But when those turn out to be dull, they start to feel like empty time themselves, which makes them dangerous.

So, to fill my empty time myself, in my own way, I'm forever stocking up on raw material, nibbling at it, swallowing it down. What lies before me becomes a mountain of raw material for filling empty time. The books I don't read, the recordings I never watch, the work I've left half done, the food I want to eat, the scenery I want to gaze at, the places I want to visit, the pleasures other people are enjoying: all of it will someday fill my empty time, and so it keeps piling up until the warehouse is full. Having my empty time filled becomes simply the way things are. And once you've done away with all that frightening empty time, you find it hard to breathe.

If any of this strikes a chord, please write in and tell me. Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today. I didn't set out to write anything gloomy. I just wrote it, that's all.
entry.summary: The essay argues that modern people, including the author, feel compelled to fill every spare moment with thinking, distraction, or planned pursuits, and that this constant filling of empty time leaves little room to breathe. It traces this restlessness back to childhood boredom, when staring at the ceiling first sparked a lifelong habit of thought.

entry.title: Don't try to beat phone scammers at their own game
entry.content:
Every so often you hear someone telling, with a certain pride, how they got one of those scam calls and "played along, pretending to be fooled, and ended up fooling the scammer instead." When I was younger, I probably would have found that hilarious, and I might even have thought I'd like to try it myself. But the person I am now would say, "You really shouldn't do that sort of thing."

People are naturally drawn to whatever is dangerous, shady, uncanny, or out of the ordinary. Perhaps that's an ability we developed for sensing danger. Or perhaps it's a spirit of adventure, the urge to blaze new trails. There's even the old saying that you can't catch the tiger's cub without going into the tiger's den. But a little knowledge is a dangerous thing. And plenty of people who go out for wool come home shorn.

It's no good, you see. At some point, how should I put it, you start taking on the same values, picking up the same rules. It happens all the time in dramas about undercover cops or spies: you breathe the same air and live the same life, and eventually you catch yourself asking, "Wait, what was the difference again?" Something you started as a joke turns serious. Look around carefully and you'll find it everywhere. I've had a few whoa-there moments of my own. Curiosity, a taste for fun, a love of adventure: these things are always tempting you to stick your nose into all sorts of places.

But I think you have to draw a line somewhere. Turning the tables on a phone scammer means you've stepped into their ring, doesn't it? You're playing their game. That's exactly why you mustn't do it.

These days, scam websites and fake articles have gotten incredibly sophisticated. Even when you come across them, you shouldn't go "pretending to be fooled" or trying to "beat" the bad guys. Stay just as you always are, and keep within your own bounds: if there's something you can actually do, do it, and leave it at that.

I know this sounds like an old man's lecture, but it matters, so I'm saying it anyway.

We'd love to hear your thoughts on this piece, too, by email.

Thanks for stopping by Hobonichi again today.

Long, long ago, Confucius, so they say, would not speak of prodigies, feats of strength, disorder, or spirits.
entry.summary: The essay argues that playing along with scammers or chasing dangerous, shady temptations is a mistake, because stepping into their world gradually erodes your own values and blurs the line between you and them. The writer urges people to stay within their own bounds and simply avoid engaging.

entry.title: What kind of company is Hobonichi, really?
entry.content:
I wonder how we, the Hobonichi crew, look to people on the outside. I wouldn't be surprised if they took us for a carefree, head-in-the-clouds sort of bunch. The struggles, the gritted teeth, the serious specialist know-how: hardly any of that shows from the outside, so I suppose it can't be helped. Then again, some people imagine the exact opposite. They figure "places like that are the ones that are secretly brutal," and picture us as some kind of ogre's lair. Well, they're free to think so, but I'd say it's neither that harsh a place nor a battlefield. When I say "everyone here is a good person," I honestly mean it, though I doubt anyone takes that at face value.

What Hobonichi is really like is hard to get across in words. I think the people who understand it best are the ones who've come in as part-timers for something like our Joy of Living Fair and worked right alongside us. It's tough, if you want to call it tough, and it's fun, if you want to call it fun. When we say "Safety first, fun second," we mean it. Then again, we also say "Health first, fun second."

Right now we're running a series of articles recruiting interns, under the title "Come along on the Hobonichi journey." New people at Hobonichi get to know the place by working with us. Spend enough time on the inside and you see just about everything, and both sides learn more about each other than any number of interviews and exams could ever reveal.

So here's the thing. As part of the reading material on that recruitment page, there's a set of crew interviews. Eight have been posted so far. Young people who joined as interns themselves sit down with other former interns, and with senior colleagues who came in through other doors. They make for really fun reading, and they feel true to life. To be honest, even I, the longest-serving member of the crew, have been enjoying them as a reader. Which makes sense, I suppose, given that the series is called "Honestly, what was hard about joining Hobonichi?"

If you're the parent, or an older friend or mentor, of someone who might apply for the internship, please feel free to let them know about it. And I'd be glad to get emails with your thoughts on this piece, too. Thanks.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi today. My cold has turned into the real thing, so I'm taking the day off work.
entry.summary: Hobonichi's staff describe their workplace as neither cold nor brutal, but a place where hard work and fun coexist and where everyone is genuinely kind. They invite prospective interns to see for themselves through a series of candid crew interviews about what joining is really like.

entry.title: Now I know about biofilm
entry.content:
A few years ago I came across the word "biofilm," and I can't help wondering how many people know it. It sounds kind of cool, doesn't it? "Bio"! "Film"! It sounds like some hot new product. You can just picture someone saying, "Oh, out on the cutting edge, everyone's gone biofilm now." That's not what it is, though.

Biofilm is the slimy stuff on your teeth. It's also the slime in your kitchen drain, and the slick coating on river rocks, the kind that sends your foot shooting right out from under you. Leave a water bottle unwashed and you'll get biofilm in there too. We already had perfectly familiar ways of describing it, the film on your teeth, the gunk in the drain, the slippery stones, and yes, that's the stuff. Apparently it's a state in which bacteria gather together and live as a community, all influencing one another. So, not cool at all. Kind of disgusting, really. It turns out bacteria find life easier in a group than on their own, so they set up house together inside that sticky structure. Gross, right? Once you know, you get a lot more serious about brushing. I brush every morning and every night now as if I'm heading into battle against biofilm.

It seems people discovered microorganisms living in the grime on teeth a whole 340 years ago, but the idea of "biofilm" only caught on in the 1970s. Can you believe it, my dear? Back when I was drawing posters for Cavity Prevention Day, I pictured germs in little devil costumes swinging pickaxes, pounding holes into teeth like they were making rice cakes. And the teacher was perfectly happy with that explanation, too. No bio, no film, nothing of the sort.

Ever since I learned about it, biofilm has been on my mind. And now that you've read this, you know too, so from here on out you'll be living in a world with biofilm in it. Sorry about that. I really didn't need to do that to you.

If you have any thoughts, please send me an email. Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today.

Learn a new word, and the world gets just a little bigger, for better or for worse...
entry.summary: The essay argues that the trendy-sounding word "biofilm" is just a fancy name for the slimy gunk we already know from teeth, drains, and slippery river rocks, and that learning new words can make the world feel bigger, for better or worse.

entry.title: Bride of the golden hairpin? I can't even read that title
entry.content:
It was Jun Miura who made the phrase "my boom" catch on. A boom, by definition, is something that sweeps up huge numbers of people, so a personal one, a "my" boom, ought to be a contradiction in terms. But these days everyone knows what it's like to have a tiny, private craze of their own, and so "my boom" became a boom in its own right. However narrow the obsession, however quickly it fizzles out, that's perfectly fine. I think part of the appeal was that you could treat the boom as disposable.

Nowadays the equivalent might be having an "oshi," someone you root for. But that word carries more emotional weight somehow, as though your whole heart is in it.

Thanks to Chiikawa, going to the movies became my boom for a while. If something looked promising, I'd book a ticket right away and just go. I had never been that light on my feet about it before. But after Godzilla -0.0, the trips to the theater stopped. The third season of Love Village started on Netflix, I got busy watching that, and from there my old boom of binge-watching dramas at home flared up all over again.

It started because Love Village 3 was so good. I could go on about it forever, but this third season is a masterpiece. It makes you feel, deep down, that every single person carries a history of their own, and thoughts and feelings that are theirs alone.

And now, for some reason, it's a Chinese drama series called Bride of the Golden Hairpin. It's a bit like the Indian films that were my boom not long ago: gorgeous, glamorous men and women driving the story forward at full throttle. To eyes grown used to a kind of next-door realism, it feels refreshing. Maybe it's the same feeling I had reading The Rose of Versailles, back in the day. Friday, Saturday, and Sunday were all consumed by Bride of the Golden Hairpin.

That said, I'm not exactly recommending it to everyone. Once you start, it gets its hooks in you and you keep watching episode after episode, but I haven't been telling the people around me, "You've got to see this." It's true that I'm watching because it's entertaining, though. It's complicated. I suppose that's about where my boom stands right now...

If you have any thoughts, please send me an email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. I'm coming down with a bit of a cold, so I'm spending the day without setting one foot outside the house.
entry.summary: The essay describes how the writer's "booms," or short-lived personal obsessions, come and go, from movies to Love Village to the Chinese drama Bride of the Golden Hairpin, and how being able to drop them easily is part of their appeal.

entry.title: On being someone who can't be bothered
entry.content:
I never had any particular philosophy about raising children, but as my daughter was growing up, I did hope she would become a child who didn't say "what a bother." Someone who wouldn't complain that things were a hassle, who wouldn't spare herself the effort. When we took the subway together, I'd ride the escalator while she climbed the stairs beside it. Somehow that just carried on, year after year, as if it were the natural order of things. Whether it's been passed down to her own daughter, I couldn't tell you.

Why did I think this way? Because I was exactly the sort of person who found everything a bother and wanted to spare himself any effort. When you have a weakness, you end up wishing the opposite on your children. Being someone who can't be bothered, who shirks effort, is no good. It's no good, and it shrinks your own possibilities. If only I'd been the kind of person who didn't hold back, I'd have had a better life... that's the sort of thing I find myself thinking.

And yet, in reality, other people describe me as the exact opposite: conscientious, eager to have a go at anything. If anything, I suspect they take me for a hard worker. But as far as I'm concerned, I find everything a bother, I begrudge every ounce of effort, I'm short on motivation, slow to get off my backside, and I'd rather be asleep, rather be lolling about. I feel as though I've lived alongside that frame of mind my whole life. That feeling is where I really come from, the true head of the household. And yet somehow, I keep ending up doing things. I even catch myself hurrying along through my ordinary days. Why on earth?!

Even today, even right now as I write this, I'm thinking what a bother it is. And yet I don't stop writing, and I've been writing every single day for more than twenty-eight years. If someone like me turned into a genuine "person who doesn't find things a bother," would I end up busier than ever with one thing and another? Hmm, that might not be such a good thing. If I went around playing at being a racing driver with my foot flat to the floor, wouldn't I wreck my own body and make a nuisance of myself to everyone around me? That's the kind of excuse I come up with, but even that seems a little suspect. I admire people who never act as though things are a bother, oh, I really, truly do. I think they're wonderful, I think they're cool, I long to be like them. And yet, somehow, I'm just not one of them.

If you have any thoughts, do send me an email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today.

Tadanori Yokoo is someone who can't be bothered, too. And look how much he paints!
entry.summary: The writer admits to finding nearly everything a bother and hoped to raise a daughter who wouldn't, yet keeps working diligently every day despite that self-image. The essay suggests that a person's self-perception and their actual conduct can diverge, and that doing things anyway can be a form of character.

entry.title: Everything changes, that much is a given, but still
entry.content:
Did the people who built the pyramids ever say to one another, "I wonder what people in the future will think when they see this"? Did they imagine, even a little, how they'd be seen? They were the ones actually building the thing, after all, so I doubt it ever crossed their minds that someone would one day ask, "How on earth did they make it?"

When I was in elementary school, a prank caught on for a while among the dumber kids: drawing fake chest hair on yourself. Back then, men like the baseball star Shigeo Nagashima, the sumo wrestler Asashio, and the leading men in foreign films all showed off their chest hair, and it looked cool. Who could have guessed that the men of later generations would get rid of so much of their body hair! Neither the kids nor the grown-ups of that time could have imagined it, not by a single hair.

The Imperial Palace in today's Chiyoda Ward stands on the site of the old Edo Castle. The people who saw that castle as part of their everyday scenery could never have imagined it would become the Imperial Palace and look the way it does now.

When you're living in a given era, you can't really understand the eras that came before it or the ones still to come. You can forecast, predict, imagine, even fantasize, if you try. But the changes almost always turn out to be on a completely different scale. Then again, we don't even understand the era we're living in...

Someday, a teacher in the far-off future might tell their students, "So up until this period, there was an institution called marriage, and people lived in units called families." Then again, teachers and students might not exist anymore either. And the language people speak will probably have changed completely.

Things change, you know, so much that it's beyond imagining. And yet, even amid all that, some things stay the same. I have a feeling that if you live with your eyes fixed on the things that don't change, the past, the present, and the future all become a little easier to see.

◆Final day's question, No. 101: "Will you keep sending me emails?"

I mean it. Write your answer in an email and send it my way, would you?

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. As for the future of the reader interviews, I'm still thinking it over. Thanks so much!
entry.summary: People living in any era cannot foresee how dramatically their world will change, from the pyramid builders to the Edo castle's transformation into the Imperial Palace. Yet even amid that constant change, the author suggests that focusing on what stays the same can make the past, present, and future easier to understand.

entry.title: Trivial things not even worth writing about
entry.content:
Give a piece the title "Trivial things not even worth writing about," and suddenly whatever you write becomes material. This is nothing more than a passing whim, but let's give it a go.

First, I wake to my iPhone alarm. It's Koji Tamaki's "Melody," and I scramble to shut it off the moment the opening words come in. Once I'm up, I sync the Oura Ring I wore overnight and check how I slept. Usually, not all that well. My sleep score is in the 70s on a good night and the 50s on a bad one, and I'm forever wishing I could pay back this thing they call sleep debt.

I take my wake-up pills with 50cc of water from the kettle. I fold the duvet in half and tidy it away. I head to the washroom, into the toilet, out again. I strip down to my underpants and weigh myself. 63 kilos. Even when it changes, it's almost always within a kilo. I don't use the word "almost" much in my writing. The "almost" in Hobonichi, whose name means "almost daily," already puts me over my maximum allowance.

I take out the mouthguard I wear because I grind my teeth. I brush, currently with a Doltz sonic toothbrush. Rather than loungewear, I get about halfway into the clothes I'll go out in. Right before I actually head out the door, I'll reconsider and add a few things.

Vegetable juice, at the moment whatever comes in a carton. Into the shaker go protein powder, dextrin, Calpis and soy milk, and I shake away while looking over the sports paper. Certain kinds of information I read with obsessive thoroughness. I glance through the print edition of the Nikkei too, but try not to read too much of it. If my "friend at home" asks me something, I'll tell her whether I'd like bread or rice; if she isn't around or doesn't ask, I figure something out myself.

Good grief, that's already about thirty minutes. All of the above happens in nearly exactly the same way every day. It's a bit like Ichiro's routine at the plate. Truly, a morning with nothing particularly happy in it, but nothing unhappy either.

◆ "The Second-to-Last Question," no. 100: "Did you enjoy the interview?"

If anything comes to mind, please write it in an email and send it along. Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today.

Actually, last night I dropped a teacup and broke it.
entry.summary: This essay is a playful, observational account of an ordinary morning, where the writer finds material in mundane routines like waking, sleep tracking, and breakfast. Its quiet insight is that a daily life with "nothing particularly happy, but nothing unhappy either" is worth noticing, and that giving small things a title is enough to make them worth writing about.

entry.title: What we have outside the walls that isn't found within
entry.content:
Yesterday I wrote that the 78 years I've lived really have been long. Not short in the least. This isn't exactly a continuation of that, but I've been thinking a little more about the length of time.

Please don't take this as anything grim. Say someone commits a crime, is tried, and goes to prison. Three years, five years, twenty years, life. That stretch of time is what we call a "sentence." During it, they should have the basics: meals, sleep, hygiene, safety. In a sense, you could say their right to live hasn't been taken from them any more than it has from the people on the outside. So what is it they don't have? Countless "freedoms."

When to eat, and what to eat. What time to go to bed and what time to get up, where to go when you step out of the house, whom to see, what to do, whether to grit your teeth through a job you hate or just skip it. Tucked inside all the things we on "the outside" do as a matter of course, without finding them the least bit remarkable, is a great heap of a precious commodity called "freedom." Simply taking most of it away is enough to make a punishment.

If someone who has done something terrible is handed, say, a sentence of five years, it means five years' worth of "freedom" is taken from them. Losing "freedom" for five years is considered heavy enough to balance out the wrong they did. And society agrees that being deprived of "freedom" for that span of time is a very great punishment indeed. This may sound like I'm being overly logical about it, but that's how enormous the value of "freedom" is!

So "freedom" is something human beings simply can't do without, I find myself thinking, rather late in the day, and getting a little sentimental about it. Well, gosh, I suppose I may be squandering my freedom a bit...

Today's question, no. 099: "When do you feel most free?"

What do you think? If you'd like, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. There's freedom in "Happy nothing-in-particular day," too, isn't there.
entry.summary: The essay argues that prison's real punishment is the loss of everyday freedoms, the countless small choices about when to eat, sleep, work, and see people, which we take for granted until they're gone. The writer reflects on how precious this freedom is and wonders whether they may be squandering their own.

entry.title: This time, the congratulations come from me
entry.content:
Once a certain amount of time has gone by, people often say, "It went by in a flash." They say things like, "It felt long, but really it was short." Today I turned seventy-eight, and let me tell you, it did not go by in a flash. Not even close. I don't for a moment think it felt long but turned out short. It's long. Seventy-eight years, in its own way, is not short at all. I want the eighteen-year-olds to know this, and the sixty-eight-year-olds too.

Every single day, you wake up and you go to sleep, you work and you play, you laugh, you grieve, you get angry, you get bored, and you do all of it, day after day. I don't remember being born, but I remember a surprising amount from when I was very small. And after that, as a boy, as a young man, and once I'd become a working adult of sorts, I've held on to it, piece by piece. And yet what I've forgotten is far, far greater.

There hasn't been a single day I spent out cold, so if you count them up one at a time, that makes 28,489 days I've been alive. Try counting on your fingers, one, two, three, four, five. Even getting to a thousand is hard work. That's folding a finger down a thousand times. It's a lot. Nobody would even try. And yet living, day by day, is something we do every day, and we keep it up for tens of thousands of days. 28,489 of them, say. It's not as if I've lived each of those days with all my might. Still, I think it's really quite something.

It feels like I've seen a lot of people off, and I've met many more. Far from going by in a flash, it's been more long days than I could ever remember. And today, one more day gets added to the pile. Pretty amazing, really.

Today's question, no. 098: "What happened for you this year?" Think back, and if you like, write it in an email and send it our way.

Thank you for coming by Hobonichi again today. Let's make today the day I celebrate you.
entry.summary: The author argues that a long life does not feel short in hindsight: each of their 28,489 days is substantial, and seventy-eight years is a long, rich span, not a flash that passed quickly.

entry.title: The distance that lets you watch with an easy heart
entry.content:
The Bungaku Free Market, the big literary fair at Tokyo Big Sight, is really something, isn't it? It was started by people who thought, "This is what we want to do," and others who felt the same way gathered around them, until it grew into something huge. I suspect they've done it almost entirely without help from professionals. I imagine they've worked hard thinking everything through: if we do it this way, this problem will come up; if that happens, we'll end up with this. But there's no such thing as a perfect event anywhere, so unless something is actually dangerous, it's fine to just do it and fix things as you go. Being an outsider, I can say that sort of thing breezily, without turning into a worrier. I feel the same way about the Hibiya Music Festival that Seiji Kameda and his team have been working so hard on all these years. Watching from a little way off, I can stay calm.

You could call that irresponsible, and maybe it is. But this kind of "watching from a distance" matters. When you're the ones running the show, a certain tension inevitably comes with it, so even with smiles on your faces, the planning and execution tend to come out a bit stiff. That said, most of what Hobonichi does seems to look like we're "just laughing our way through it." I think that's sort of our signature.

This time, the writers of Hobonichi's "3-Minute Column" have been busily pitching in on what amounts to a volunteer basis, and since the venue is only open for a short time, everyone seems relaxed in their own way. This is going to be a good experience for them. They've got a booth, and they made books to sell, but their participation has a slightly hobbyist feel to it. Watching the other booths and the way the organizers run things from that kind of distance must have been a real education. Making, selling, buying, wandering around, keeping watch: whatever role people were in, I bet they were all using their imagination to picture what it's like for those in the other roles.

As for me personally, it was the first time in a while that I spent hours locked in battle with the call of nature.

◆Today's question, no. 097: "Who do you want to see right now?" Simple as that. If you like, write your answer in an email and send it in.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. It's nice, too, that the rest of the Hobonichi crew went along to look around and cheer them on.
entry.summary: This essay reflects on the Bungaku Free Market and Hobonichi's volunteer-run participation, arguing that a relaxed, slightly outsider stance, rather than anxious perfectionism, lets people enjoy and learn from community-driven events while still picturing the perspectives of everyone involved.

entry.title: Here I am, at my age, still saying things like this
entry.content:
I started something I call "Chiikawa rinsho," copying Chiikawa drawings the way calligraphy students copy from a master's model, and I still haven't quit. Nobody has actually told me, "You'll never stick with it." But I'm sure somebody would, so from the very start I've been stubbornly refusing to quit (ha). Well, if I'm honest, the one most likely to say it is me. But it's still going, you hear that, self?

Doing something every day is genuinely fascinating. When you repeat more or less the same thing over and over, the "extra thinking," the quibbling and the excuses, starts to fall away. That alone makes it good training for me.

Rinsho doesn't ask you to be original in the first place. Some individuality is bound to slip through, but the idea is simply to write it the way the model shows you. Chiikawa rinsho is drawing rather than lettering, but it's the same in that you're following the path a brush or pen traveled. Someone like me, though, short on both spirit and skill, can't actually follow that movement. It's probably like copying your dance teacher's moves and still not really dancing. I'm supposedly looking right at the model, yet I'm not seeing it. I suppose I could just trace where the lines and dots fall, but then the motion, the thing that actually happened there, would freeze in place and die. And since I don't have the posture or the technique for that motion, I can't move the brush or pen the way I mean to. Dots, circles, straight lines: I can't draw a single one of them properly.

Having said all that, I'm not discouraged. I'm drawing again today. I post them on Twitter like I'm handing in homework, and some people kindly tell me, "You're getting better!" To which I say: oh no, not at all, but I'm not stopping. And once again it hits me how wonderful the teacher who drew the originals really is.

◆Today's question no. 096: "What are you learning, or imitating?" Have a think. If you like, send your answer by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. Whether it's singing or dancing, I guess getting the shape right just isn't enough.
entry.summary: The writer describes daily copying of Chiikawa drawings as a discipline that quiets their self-doubt, even though they feel they cannot truly capture the original's spirit and motion. They suggest that faithfully reproducing a model's form falls short of really learning it.

entry.title: As I kept writing, it took a turn
entry.content:
Children are fools. Or rather, children do foolish things. This is a theory I arrived at through my own experience, but it has only grown sturdier the more I've heard other people's stories.

If you jump off something high while holding an open umbrella, you'll float gently down and won't get hurt. Most kids (mostly boys, I'd guess) must have believed this right up until they tried it. Still, one attempt is all it takes to reach the correct conclusion.

They collect things with no idea what they're collecting them for. Pill bugs, bagworms, some kind of trading card, stickers, whatever it is, they set about collecting it. However many years they keep at it, at some point they've simply stopped. Nobody knows why they stopped, but then nobody knows why they started, either. What you come to realize is that the very idea of a reason doesn't exist for them.

As a rule, big things are better and small things are worse. That's the verdict, and it gets applied in every situation imaginable. "Huge!" is a compliment, and in most situations they'd like to be huge themselves.

As I slowly dredge up memories like these, there's something I can't help noticing, whether I like it or not. I started out talking about children, but adults, even if they dip it all in batter and deep-fry it, are pretty much the same, aren't they? Adults are fools too. Or rather, adults do foolish things too.

It isn't only an adult living inside an adult. Some unchanging child ingredient is mixed in there, living on inside the adult-shaped container. And that brings good things, bad things, and awkward things. Just because you've grown up doesn't mean you get to go around acting clever.

◆ Today's question, if you'll pardon the intrusion, No. 095: "Am I a fool?" Give it some thought, and if you feel like it, write it up in an email and send it our way.

Thanks for stopping by Hobonichi again today. Maybe the very heart that says "yeah, me too" is what qualifies you as a grown-up.
entry.summary: The essay argues that children's foolishness is a universal trait that never fully disappears, and adults remain foolish too, with a childlike part of everyone persisting beneath the grown-up exterior. Recognizing that shared foolishness, the author suggests, is itself a mark of maturity.

entry.title: Well, let's have some tea and chat...
entry.content:
Whenever someone says, "Not to brag or anything, but...", there's usually at least a little bragging mixed in. Or am I wrong?

People say, "We hope all you folks at home will enjoy this," but where exactly are all these homes, I wonder. I'm sure they exist somewhere. I'd just love, one time, to gather them all in one place and take a good look.

Oh, right. Not to brag or anything, but in this precious life of mine, I try never to go without something made with anko, that sweet red bean paste. Sometimes it's this or that from Toraya, sometimes Akafuku from Ise, sometimes Hanazono Manju from Shinjuku, sometimes the hot-spring buns from Seihotei in Ikaho, sometimes dorayaki from Usagiya in Ueno, sometimes dorayaki from Kamejyu in Asakusa, sometimes mame daifuku from Mizuho in Harajuku, sometimes mame daifuku from Matsushimaya in Takanawa, sometimes taiyaki from Naniwaya in Azabu-Juban, sometimes anpan from Kimuraya in Ginza, sometimes Yamadaya buns from Uwa, sometimes bamboo-leaf dumplings from Tanakaya in Niigata, sometimes Mosuke dango from Toyosu... and there are plenty more, but those are the ones that spring to mind right away.

Some I can pick up nearby, some require a little outing, some I bring back as souvenirs, some are gifts, some I order by mail. On top of that, I sometimes make anko myself. In any case, life without red bean sweets would be a real problem.

The other day, though, I learned that Kashiwaya in Fukushima, makers of the thin-skinned buns I adore, had switched to packaging that keeps longer, so I bought a whole batch. And because they were reliably there every single day, my gratitude faded, and they stopped thrilling me the way they used to. I've been reflecting on that.

Even in days so devoted to red bean sweets, there comes the occasional day when I simply want a Western-style cake. So today I bought a strawberry shortcake and ate it.

Today's question, no. 094: "Go ahead, write whatever you like." Not sure what to say? If you feel like it, write it in an email and send it our way.

Thanks for stopping by Hobonichi again today. You know, the frozen imagawayaki they sell at convenience stores are surprisingly good, too.
entry.summary: The writer, a devoted lover of red bean sweets, reflects on how the constant availability of their favorite treats has dulled their delight, revealing how familiarity can quietly erode gratitude and joy.

entry.title: Writing this down as a warning to myself (ha)
entry.content:
Maybe parents and teachers are different these days, but for my generation, and for a generation or so after mine, adults were forever handing out warnings. "Don't get full of yourself." "Don't get complacent." "Nothing is ever easy." "You're not trying hard enough." "Don't you dare take this lightly." We heard it constantly. Having spent my life steeped up to the neck in admonitions meant to keep me from going easy on myself, I eventually got into the habit of telling myself not to get full of myself. Whenever I set out to do something, I furrow my brow and think, "This is going to be hard." Even when things are going well, I lecture myself: "Get cocky and you'll fall flat on your face." I'm not saying this about the world at large. That stuff is sloshing around inside me, filled right to the brim. That's how I was raised, and that's how I've lived.

Still, if you live like that, you never get anything done. And I didn't want to become the kind of person who's always frightening or scolding other people about whatever they're trying to do. So I've gone through life tossing off jokes like, "Is the world sweet or sour? You'll never know until you give it a lick."

Calmly scanning for oversights, for hidden pitfalls, makes a person look smart, so plenty of people are eager to do it. And since everyone dreads hearing "I told you so" when they fail, clever people like to be the ones doing the checking. But there's no point in having everybody crowded over on that side. I'll say it again: I'm prone to ending up on that side myself.

That's not the way! Something that seems difficult can turn out to be the other side of the very same coin as something you can do if you just try. You shouldn't take things lightly, but you won't get anywhere if you're afraid. Even the work you do with a furrowed brow can be done while laughing. For some reason, I felt like writing all that down again.

Today's question no. 093: "Have you ever gotten full of yourself?" Think back. If you like, please send us your answer by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today.

The man who tapped the stone bridge so many times to make sure it was safe that he broke it, and had no choice but to swim across the moat...
entry.summary: The author describes being raised on constant warnings against complacency, which left them scolding themselves before every task and always checking for pitfalls. They conclude that difficulty and ease are two sides of the same coin, and that one can take things seriously while still doing them with a laugh.

entry.title: Staff meals, home cooking, and the pleasures of everyday life
entry.content:
Of course there's nothing wrong with the "supreme flavors" of famous, wildly acclaimed restaurants, or with places boasting however many Michelin stars. But what I really want to eat is the staff meals and home cooking of the people who make that kind of food. I know plenty of them will say, "Oh, I don't cook at home," and if that's the case, then I'd like to try whatever good little place in the neighborhood they love.

This idea has been pretty fundamental to me ever since I started Hobonichi. When I launched a series with Takaaki Yoshimoto, a thinker known for being notoriously difficult, I even titled it "Takaaki Yoshimoto's Staff Meals." Not a showpiece made with expensive ingredients and no effort spared, but the everyday food someone sets in front of you with a casual "Stay and eat." That's the kind of thing you can keep close company with for a long time. Sure, the high-end, the lavish, the delicate, the supreme, the ultimate, they're all fine. But somehow, what I look forward to is "the usual."

Recently I came across a manga series called Nishimochi's Everyday. Apart from the work the artist produces as a professional cartoonist, there's this one extra line devoted to drawing daily life. It's done diary-style, in simple lines, and yet reading it feels like having a pleasant conversation with someone you're close to. Yes, it's exactly that: a staff meal, home cooking.

Come to think of it, Yuko Higuchi's Boris Picture Diary, a loose, easygoing four-panel strip about everyday life, was wonderful too, and Ayako Ishiguro's Tenmaru and Family Picture Diary was genuinely funny and I adored it. But both of them stopped at a certain point. I suspect maybe they quit "before it turned into real work," but as a reader, I'd have happily kept reading them forever. Work that's made lightly, almost offhandedly, like home cooking, with no intention of impressing anyone: I like it so much that I'd almost say I prefer it.

Today's question, no. 092: "What's your favorite snack, or your favorite thing to nibble on with a drink?" Give it a little thought. If you'd like, write it in an email and send it our way.

Thank you for coming by Hobonichi again today. Now that I think of it, our Everyday Pleasures Fair might be something along the same lines.
entry.summary: The essay argues that ordinary, unpretentious everyday food and creative work, like a staff meal or home cooking, often matter more than the lavish and acclaimed, because they offer a warm, lasting sense of companionship. The author illustrates this through Hobonichi's projects and diary-style manga that feel like casual conversation with a friend.

entry.title: More on the reader interviews, and other things
entry.content:
The "reader interview" I've been running at the end of these short pieces is getting close to its hundredth question. Which is to say, that's where it ends. After doing it a hundred days in a row, I have to admit it's a little sad to see it go. Especially for me, you know. The interview takes up three lines, so I'd been trimming the writing that came before it. At first I couldn't get used to that, but little by little I did, and along the way I picked up a "somewhat freer" way of writing. It's probably hard for anyone else to notice, but I'd loosened up a bit. If I go back to the original twenty-seven characters by forty lines, I suspect I'll struggle with that in its own way.

Now, there's something I should tell you ahead of time. I'd planned to stop at question 100, on that very day, but I've decided to keep the interview going for one more. The reason is that no. 074, "Is there a place you're a regular at?", and no. 040, "Is there a place you always go back to?", were far too similar. I thought I'd been careful to come up with questions that didn't overlap with ones I'd already asked, but I slipped up. Truth is, I ask similar things all the time. Then again, that happens plenty even when you're talking face to face with someone, so I'd been letting it slide. This time, though, I wanted a do-over. So question 101 will run on November 13th, and that will be the end.

I'll probably talk about this project again once it wraps up, but interviews really are curious occasions, aren't they? There are things you'd never have thought about if nobody had asked, and sometimes being asked leads you to discover something about yourself. I've been on both sides, asking and being asked, and even now I often find myself stopping short and thinking, "Huh, so that's how I saw it."

And then there's something Satoru Iwata used to say a lot, too: "Once it's written down, you end up sounding like you're full of yourself." There's that tendency, and I really can't stand it. The more honestly and plainly you answer, the more likely you are to come off sounding cocky. I've even been known to ask for my blunt sentence endings to be swapped out for polite ones, you know (ha).

◆Today's question, no. 091: "Memories of this summer..." (ha)

Not bad, right? If you feel like it, send me your answer by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. December mode is slowly creeping up on us. It's like this every year.
entry.summary: The writer is ending a hundred-day "reader interview" feature, reflecting on how the daily discipline loosened their writing style and how being asked questions reveals things about oneself. They also decide to extend the run by one question to fix a repeated question, marking the close of the project.

entry.title: Losing, losing, losing, losing, and winning now and then?
entry.content:
I can't say everyone has it, but it seems like an awful lot of people do. It isn't an instinct anymore, and yet it's a desire that comes very close to one. I think of it as the hunger to win. People just want to win, plain and simple. Or maybe what it really comes down to is that they can't stand to stay beaten. Even in some trivial argument, people try to win, and they mean it. It's the kind of thing people tease each other about, calling it "lose-and-you-die syndrome."

A lot of the time it isn't even about ourselves. We root for an athlete or a team and want them to win. We want it desperately, as if we'd come apart if they lost. The things we own, the place we were born: there too, we simply want to win. Once it's between countries, or religion or ideology gets mixed in, that wanting-to-win gets tangled up in conflicts as well. And people who come to grief through gambling probably started out the same way, with "I can't stay beaten" or "I want to win," until they reached a point where they couldn't back out.

In ordinary life, people don't actually win very much (even sumo wrestlers don't win every bout). If anything, we're forever aware of having lost, or of not measuring up. So we need to be winning at something just to keep ourselves going. It can be sports, it can be your favorite idol hitting it big, it can be a big payout at the horse races, it can be your son's Little League game. Somewhere, at something, we want to win so that things balance out. I think that's what's going on (this is a theory I came to by watching myself, mind you). Since those of us out here in the world are mostly not winning, maybe we're buying our wins, spending money and so on to get them. That said, I don't know whether it works the same way for women.

◆Today's question no.090: "Is there anything you're winning at?"

What do you think? Give it some thought, and if you'd like, send us your answer by email.

Thank you for coming by Hobonichi again today. Things that aren't instincts but act just like them, they're out there, aren't they.
entry.summary: The essay argues that the urge to win, something close to an instinct, drives people to need some victory in life to offset their everyday sense of losing, whether through sports, a favorite celebrity, a bet, or a child's achievement. It suggests this hunger can even fuel conflicts and compulsions like gambling.

entry.title: What people are capable of, for better or worse
entry.content:
There are things I think I understand in my head, and yet, if I'm honest, I somehow still don't really get them. Take "personal information," which comes up so often these days. I haven't quite sorted out what I think about it. Your name and address, plus your phone number (or these days, I suppose, your email address), count as important "personal information." That much I understand perfectly well. Naturally, it would be a problem if they were used by bad people.

But when you have a pizza or some takeout delivered, they know your phone number, your address, your name, and very nearly your face. Maybe you sometimes order under a fake name, and maybe the handoff can happen without anyone seeing anyone, but on the whole it's normal to assume they know who you are. The person who puts letters in your mailbox can deliver them precisely because they know your name and address. It's not a pleasant way to put it, but your "personal information," and mine, isn't known only to the people we know.

And, speaking strictly in terms of logic, if someone you know were to become an "enemy," your "personal information" would remain in the hands of someone you'd rather didn't have it. If I may push the logic a little further: however close a company comes to perfect security, if a person who works near some crucial secret decides to leak it, that "information" can no longer be protected, just like that.

This is a very TV-drama sort of example, but if there were information you truly wanted to steal, one method might even be to become the person that company or organization needs most, and simply get yourself inside. At the level of nations and defense, I suppose that's what spies do.

I'm someone who would rather not believe that people are bad by nature, but logically speaking, human beings carry a potential, for better or worse, that can rival the failure of any vast system. Yes, "for better or worse," people are magnificent, and terrifying. And yet trying to live without trusting people is also very, very hard.

◆Today's question, no. 089: "How do you like your eggs?" What do you think? If you'd like, please send us your answer by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. I think we'll spend our whole lives thinking about nothing but people.
entry.summary: The essay argues that "personal information" is never truly contained, since anyone who serves us, from delivery workers to insiders, can access it, so the real vulnerability lies in human nature and the trust we must place in others anyway.

entry.title: Find a question, and you can't help wanting to answer it
entry.content:
When some people spot a problem, they want to solve it. I suspect there are more of them than you'd think. Satoru Iwata, who was president of Nintendo, was one of them. Put something in front of him that was clearly a problem, and he'd immediately start working out a solution, and then go ahead and carry it out.

Even in conversation, if you asked him something, he'd try to answer it seriously. Even when it hadn't quite taken the form of a question, if he sensed there was a question hidden somewhere inside it, he'd go looking for the answer. People with that sort of instinct, he once told me, "are pretty common among engineers and programmers."

Come to think of it, whenever Iwata-san was coming over, I always made a point of piling all kinds of snacks on the table, right where he could see them. I'd told everyone at Hobonichi: "To Iwata-san, the snacks in front of him are a problem. He'll try to solve it, so he'll keep eating them." The result was always the same. The snacks would, without fail, disappear. For people like that, a problem is a snack. However hard it is, they can't resist wanting to work it out.

There's a reason this story came back to me. Lately, the resident Goddess of Disposal in our house has been weaving large patterns out of colorful vinyl tape. They're pieces for the Knitting Suzu Project, an earthquake recovery effort I've been doing together with Kodue Hibino. The round pieces everyone makes, something like little rugs, will decorate the walls of a dining hall in Suzu where the townspeople gather.

Until now, volunteers had been coming together at Hobonichi to make them, but we've also started accepting pieces sent in from all over the country. And our Goddess of Disposal has been knitting away at them with great enthusiasm. The announcement was hard to find, even on Hobonichi, so I asked her, "What made you decide to do it?" Her answer was simple: "They'd put out the pattern."

See the pattern (the question, the snack), and you knit it (answer it, eat it). Ah, so that's how it works, I thought, and found myself remembering Iwata-san.

Today's question, no. 088: "What kind of face do you have?" Have a think, and if you like, send us your answer by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. If you're up for it, we'd love your help with the vinyl tape knitting.
entry.summary: People who instinctively try to solve any problem they see, like Nintendo's Satoru Iwata, are more common than one might think. The author compares this drive to a snack set in front of them: irresistible to work through, just as a knitting pattern invites volunteers to take it up.

entry.title: On getting along
entry.content:
You know those videos where a mother dog or cat introduces her babies to a person she's come to trust? I've seen a few of them. I can't know what she's actually feeling, but from our side, the human side, I can't help reading it my own way: "I wanted you to meet them. These are my little ones, my precious, precious babies. Please be good to them." It looks as though she's bringing together the children she treasures and someone she knows she can rely on.

We're always being encouraged to mix: across industries, across cultures, to bring different kinds of people together. And why is it so pleasant to watch creatures of different species getting along? Unlikely pairs of animals playing together, eating together, one nursing the other's young... When a video shows me that yes, this really can happen, I can't help feeling glad.

Mind you, animals of the same kind getting along warm the heart plenty, too. Yes, I suppose anything getting along stirs up a kind of pleasure in whoever's watching. Watching children play together makes me happy somehow, and it's lovely to see a child doting on a pet or a doll.

Everybody loves seeing others get along. But, well, in real life, getting along doesn't seem all that easy. Not getting along looks like the simpler, safer choice, and perhaps it even pays off now and then. I wonder whether getting along is something a person can learn.

Today's question, no. 087: "Are you getting along?" And with whom? Give it some thought, and if you like, tell us by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today.

What if you could take lessons in getting along, the way you can with a musical instrument or painting?
entry.summary: The essay observes that watching animals, children, or people of different kinds get along brings a quiet joy, yet getting along is hard in real life, and the writer wonders whether it's a skill that can be learned.

entry.title: The kind of thing even I'd forget if I didn't write it down
entry.content:
What I'm about to write is truly trivial, utterly beside the point. It's just that if I don't write it, it will stay unwritten forever, and somehow that felt like a bit of a shame, so I decided to write it. What's more, I made this resolution while squatting on the toilet... a real bottom-line decision, you might say.

Here goes: I want a bread machine again. Not a toaster. I mean the electric gadget that bakes bread starting from flour. There may still be one lying around somewhere in the house, but I suspect the one I bought last time has been thrown out. Naturally, since it sat unused for years and years. I can't imagine that my boss at home, who is enshrined here as the Deity of Discarding, would have let it sit there unnoticed.

That's right, I've bought one before. Actually, I bought one before that, too. Over the course of my long life, I've bought maybe five bread machines... or I might be padding the count by one. Let's say four times, then, I bought one, got bored with it, and it was either forgotten or thrown away.

And now I've stumbled on a reason to want one, just a little. A specialty baking-supplies shop was selling "bread mix" flour. Oh, so you can buy the flour here, I thought. I bet it's delicious. And the instant that tiny thought crossed my mind, the smell of fresh-baked bread came billowing through my brain. It doesn't keep well, but straight out of the machine, it's the best. And then the bonus came charging in: "It makes mochi, too!" I mean, come on. Now I'm hungry for it. That's just where I'm at.

It isn't even expensive, only a little over ten thousand yen. If I were an old man living alone, I'd buy one this very minute. But I'm not, and my boss reads these ramblings too. "Obviously not! Honestly, the very idea!" So I'm not buying one. A bread machine? Absolutely not. And even if, hypothetically, I did buy one, I'd hide it somewhere and, picking a moment when the boss is out, quickly bake a loaf on the sly. Though, you know, I don't think the boss would actually object to eating it. Maybe I'll borrow one from someone at Hobonichi, a bread machine...

◆ Today's question, no. 086: "Purchases you agonize over." Do you have any? Give it some thought, and if you'd like, send us an email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. There's an old saying, you know: on Thursdays, read something silly.
entry.summary: The writer, after impulsively deciding to finally write down a trivial wish, admits a craving for a bread machine sparked by the idea of fresh-baked loaves and mochi, then talks themselves out of buying one because of their boss's disapproval and their history of abandoning past machines. It's a playful, self-deprecating take on the tug-of-war between a small indulgence and the reasons to resist it.

entry.title: Do you love a good chance? That's a chance too
entry.content:
At the "Dojo," our weekly gathering for what we call deadly serious, super-casual chitchat, we got to talking about what a wonderful thing a "chance" is. Everybody loves a chance. I do too. It's a word that's been tossed around in a pretty ordinary way for as long as anyone can remember, and we all use it as if we know exactly what it means, but somehow it feels like more than plain "luck."

What came to mind for me during that conversation was an example from soccer: when a player spots some space, an open patch of the field, and uses it to carry the play forward, you could say he's found a chance. That led us back to something we'd talked about the other day, the idea that "sense is the ability to find chances."

When I looked up "chance" again, I found it described as a word for an "opportunity" or "possibility" to do something, or else for "accident" or "likelihood." Apparently in English people tend to reach for "opportunity" when they mean the hopeful sense, but who cares? If accidents can be found, I'd like to go looking for them too.

Finding a "possibility" means, in other words, finding "hope." Even when you're stuck and can't move, when the losses keep piling up, when everything has felt like one long overcast sky, a sudden gust of wind can sometimes push those dark clouds aside. Noticing that wind is what a "chance" is, isn't it? If you can see even the faintest possibility of trying something, it leads you toward "hope" in a way that staying flattened never will.

Don't we all love a story like that? You and I, in ways big and small, have kept finding this chance and that chance, and that's how we've made it through to the next day, toward the future, haven't we? Come to think of it, that's what Hobonichi has been doing all along. "I want us to be a team that finds chances and makes chances," is where our conversation ended up.

Today's question, no. 085: "Do you remember a chance of some kind?" Think back, and if you'd like, write it up in an email and send it our way.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. It's a little late to be saying so, but that song "Give Peace a Chance" really is a good one.
entry.summary: A casual weekly chat about the word "chance" leads to the idea that a chance is a glimmer of possibility that lifts us out of stagnation and gives us hope. The essay suggests that sense is the ability to notice these openings and that we get through hard times by finding and making them.

entry.title: A voice grown old, a voice that won't carry
entry.content:
Age and aging aren't unrelated. There's certainly a connection. But it isn't anything like a neat, direct proportion. Each of us, of course, sinks deeper into old age at our own pace. In my case, too, it's been creeping along, slowly, little by little. Cataloguing every symptom wouldn't make for interesting reading, but there is one thing I find genuinely sad.

My voice. The muscles of the vocal cords lose their elasticity like everything else, so the instrument I use to make sound has undoubtedly grown old. But I was always someone with a naturally big voice. Without my thinking about it much, it carried a long way. It rang, you might say. I knew it had helped me enormously when it came to communicating. I didn't have to try very hard, and my voice reached people, got through to them. Long before I ever had to wrestle with phrasing or how to put my words together, getting that voice to land, near or far, took no effort at all. That made life easy.

But at some point, I can't quite say when, my voice became harder to hear. The sound that comes out, in both volume and quality, is weaker than what I'm trying to say. If it were too strong, I could bring it down and keep it in check. But I can tell for myself that the tone, the volume, the color of it all feel unreliable. And right there, what little confidence I had shrinks a bit further. There are good days and bad days, it's true. But on the whole, I no longer feel that my voice could reach very far.

Compared with all the other signs of aging, people don't talk about this one much, but watching your voice lose its quality and its strength is a lonely thing. There are glasses for the eyes and hearing aids for the ears, but wanting to be heard doesn't mean you can go around with a megaphone. It isn't that I want to be loud. The ideal is to have a big, clear, ringing voice and be able to use it softly. I have karaoke coming up soon, so this is what's been on my mind.

Today's question is no. 084: "What doesn't go the way you want it to?" If something comes to mind, please send it to us by email, if you'd like.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi today. I have a feeling vocal warm-ups are better done in a low voice.
entry.summary: The writer reflects on how aging has quietly weakened their once naturally powerful voice, leaving them feeling unheard and lonely in a way people rarely discuss. They wish to still be able to use their voice with softness and clarity rather than force.

entry.title: Don't bully an AI, or a loofah, or an octopus, for that matter
entry.content:
Apparently there's such a thing as "bullying AI." I suppose it takes all sorts of forms: hurling the kind of abuse you could never say to another human being, doing something nasty in the middle of an ongoing conversation, feeding it false information, and so on. The AI, presumably, doesn't get "hurt" by any of this, and if you asked it, "Does that hurt you?", the AI itself would tell you, "I don't experience being hurt." The flip side of bullying AI is thanking it, but apparently that doesn't make it "happy" either. Some people even say that just trading thank-yous is a waste of energy resources.

I'm not trying to play the good guy here, but I don't want to bully AI, and I don't intend to. And while it may not be the correct thing to do, I say thank you to AI, and I'll keep on saying it. You might be thinking, what's the point of that? But for me there's meaning in it, and purpose, and reason, and conviction, and even a certain pleasure. I can explain it in my own way, so let me give it a try.

Put as simply as I can, it comes down to this. It's the same with a dog or a cat: doing that sort of thing dirties your own soul. Even if the other side isn't listening, the soul of the one doing the talking gets dirty. You become the soul of someone who says things like that. And a soul like that starts living that way. I don't want that, so I don't want to do it. That's all there is to it.

To put it in slightly more scientific-sounding terms, if you apply a force to something (action), the same force ought to come back at you (reaction). Whether it's a person, a dog, a cat, a wall, or an AI, every action has its reaction. That's my explanation. It's an image I find myself using quite a lot. Like how the bill for whatever you've done usually shows up a little late, you know?

◆ Today's question is No. 083: "Are there days when you feel lonely?" Have a think, and if you'd like, send us your answer by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. I'd like AI and robots and the rest to get along well with people, too.
entry.summary: The author argues they choose to thank AI and avoid bullying it, not because the AI feels anything, but because mistreating anything, including AI, dirties one's own soul and reshapes one's character, with the harm eventually returning like a delayed bill.
